sourceReviews.independentSolution: Reuse d280: from the front-wall side hole, the beam in clean air is not visible in the intended negligible-visible-scattering model, because the unredirected beam travels between the side-wall holes rather than into the eye. Clean does not imply literally zero scattering; sufficiently strong side scattering or a different observation path can alter visibility. A lit wall/hole is not the beam path in air.

coverage.evidence: Visible /0 retains the apparatus and viewing direction, but neither true option A nor D states the intended conditional nonvisibility prediction. See D293-F001.

sourceReviews.independentSolution: Reuse d280: a Sun-viewing observer inside the lunar penumbra sees a partial solar eclipse. Some, not all, rays from the extended solar disk are intercepted by the Moon. Merely having some part of Earth in that region does not place every terrestrial observer there.

coverage.evidence: Visible /1 A retains the local partial-disk prediction; C separates an unlocated observer from the Earth-overall statement. The additional location distinction supports rather than substitutes for the eclipse task.

sourceReviews.independentSolution: Reuse d280: an effective small aperture produces a camera-obscura scene image by near-straight rays crossing at the opening; upper/lower and left/right object coordinates reverse on the opposite screen. An opening small in both transverse directions supports a resolved two-dimensional scene; a long unrestricted slit need not. Colors can come from the illuminated objects' own reflected light. A literal dispersed spectrum is not established by the literary rainbow description.

coverage.evidence: Visible /2 preserves the dark room, gap, opposite wall, inverted rooftops/trees/clothes and color explanation. A tests aperture-conditioned upper-to-lower crossing and D tests scene colors without compulsory dispersion. It does not replace the explanation with only a complaint about missing aperture dimensions.

limitations: Only one transverse crossing is explicit in the choices; recognition is not a written construction of both coordinate mappings.
No actual aperture size or real image is verified. Literal-spectrum HOLD remains conditional and is not cleared.

sourceReviews.independentSolution: Reuse d280: a finite emitting region gives displaced shadow edges and a penumbra. Feet are near the ground screen, so displacement is small; the head is farther from that screen, so penumbra broadens. For the same local finite-source geometry, w approximately equals D b/a. An ideal point source has no source-size penumbra.

coverage.evidence: Visible /3 C couples finite emitter size with both foot/head distances and the correct narrow/wide comparison; it does not replace edge sharpness with brightness or inverse-square distance alone.

sourceReviews.independentSolution: Reuse d280, without rerunning its arithmetic: 1.6 m from 80 cd and 2.0 m from 125 cd; normal direct illuminance is 31.25 lx per opposite face. At the screen center, the opposite rays and opposite receiving normals give equal incidence-angle cosines. A common positive cosine leaves this balance position unchanged. At cosine zero, both ideal direct illuminances vanish at every interior position and equality is nonunique.

coverage.evidence: Visible /4 A and C retain both positive distances and the nonzero-tilt result; D separately retains the grazing zero degeneracy. No original numerical value, source identity or second subquestion is omitted.

Below the midpoint each contribution is 600/(13 sqrt(13)) lx, total 1200/(13 sqrt(13)) lx. Both lights contribute at every point and the oblique cosine is required.

taskFidelity.evidence: The source asks whether the side observer can see this beam. A only states a necessary condition for seeing; D says visibility depends on scattering strength and conditions. No true option applies the intended negligible-visible-scattering model to predict nonvisibility. Someone who still believes a beam is ordinarily visible side-on in clean air can consistently select A,D, reject the literal-zero-scattering claim B and reject the direct-exit direction C. This is a removed prediction, not merely the unavoidable loss of free-response writing.

redundancy.evidence: A concerns light reaching the eye; D concerns how much scattering reaches it and detection. These are related necessary/contingent distinctions within one setup, not duplicate questions or reliance on another answer. This does not compensate for the missing prediction.

answerLeakage.evidence: The stem supplies hole geometry and clean-air wording, not an answer or option IDs. B's strict no-scattering assertion and C's front/exit conflation are physically false, not declared false by a supplied key. The generic A,D route bypasses the source prediction as recorded under fidelity; no separate author-key leak is established.

mathematics.independentSolution: For the visible claims, seeing a path requires light from it to reach the eyes. Clean air can still scatter, so its label alone does not force a strict impossibility at every brightness. The front-wall side view is not the continuation through the opposite side-wall exit hole. Visibility depends on side-scattered signal and observation conditions. These facts establish A,D, but do not establish the source's intended nonvisibility outcome under a specified approximation.

optionChecks.evidence: Without any path-originating light entering the eye there is no visual signal from that path. This is necessary, not sufficient to predict visibility.

The inference clean air implies exactly zero scattering is false. Nonzero molecular scattering is compatible with clean air; negligible ordinary visibility is an approximation, not strict impossibility at all intensities.
The beam joins the side-wall hole and opposite-wall hole. A front-wall eye is side-on, not along that exit continuation; light must be redirected toward that eye to show the path.
Side-scattered flux reaching the eye and its detectability affect seeing a beam. A weak undetectable signal and a strong detectable signal can differ even if both air samples are clean.

bilingual.evidence: Both /0 arrays keep the side/opposite/front distinction, strict zero scattering in B and visibility dependence in D. The same missing source prediction affects both languages.

taskFidelity.evidence: A directly answers the original eclipse-appearance task for the penumbra observer. C prevents the Earth-overall wording from being misread as locating every observer. Locating the observer is a physically necessary scope clarification; it does not replace partial-disk geometry with only an underdetermination question.

redundancy.evidence: A tests local occultation; B/C test an unjustified all-Earth inference and D tests total versus partial coverage. These are distinct relationships within one source task; no other question supplies the lunar-shadow answer.

answerLeakage.evidence: The stem names the penumbra but does not define it as partial solar coverage or specify a correct set. A versus D still requires the optical distinction between penumbra and full shadow; C requires an observer-location distinction.

mathematics.independentSolution: Use the usual Sun-viewing observer implicit in this solar-eclipse question, with penumbra distinct from umbra/antumbra. At an interior penumbral location, the Moon intercepts some solar-disk rays while others reach the observer: A. Earth's overlap with that region does not locate an arbitrary observer: C. An observer outside the eclipse region is a counterexample to B. Total disk blockage belongs to an umbral observer, not this penumbral one: D is false.

optionChecks.evidence: Partial interception of an extended solar disk is exactly the penumbral eclipse view; some direct solar light remains.
Some Earth region in lunar penumbra does not put every observer there. A location outside the eclipse track need not see any solar occultation.
Earth's regional overlap alone leaves the particular observer unlocated; different observer locations can have different occultation or none.
Blocking the entire solar disk contradicts the partially unblocked ray bundle defining this penumbra. It is not the local view in A.

bilingual.evidence: Both languages separate an observer inside the lunar penumbra from merely some region of Earth entering it. Partial/entire solar-disk quantifiers and unspecified observer position correspond.

taskFidelity.evidence: A gives the aperture-conditioned upper-scene to lower-wall path explaining inversion, while D gives a non-dispersive explanation of the scene's colors. Both requested explanatory components remain. A does not claim that an arbitrary long slit resolves all scene points; its sufficient-direction-restriction clause is a genuine condition, not a substitute question asking only whether more data are needed.

redundancy.evidence: A/B contrast ray-crossing image formation with compulsory lenses. C/D contrast object colors with compulsory spectral splitting. These are the two source phenomena, not two repeats of the same answer.

answerLeakage.evidence: The stem reports the observed inversion and colored scene, as the source does, but does not supply the mechanism. Rejecting a compulsory lens and a compulsory spectrum requires counterexamples. A and D do not depend on another question or an exposed solution.

mathematics.independentSolution: In the d280 small-aperture geometric model, a ray through the opening at the origin from an object point of height y at positive object distance u reaches a wall at positive image distance v with image height -(v/u)y. The analogous horizontal coordinate also reverses. A is a qualified possible path, not an unconditional sharp-image claim for every gap. A lens is unnecessary: a pinhole is a counterexample to B. Colored scene light can form a colored image without a disperser, falsifying C's claimed sufficiency and supporting D.

optionChecks.evidence: For a sufficiently direction-limiting aperture, near-straight continuation through the opening maps an upper object point to a lower wall point. The option says if/can; it does not assert this resolution for every unspecified slit.
A small pinhole and an opposite screen produce an inverted object image with no lens. This supplies a direct counterexample to the option's impossibility.
A pinhole imaging differently colored objects yields a colored picture without splitting white light into a spectrum. Thus rainbow-like colors alone do not establish dispersion as its cause.
The objects' reflected spectral distributions can remain distinguishable through the opening. Their spatial image colors do not require a prism, grating or other white-light disperser.

bilingual.evidence: Both /2 A options use a conditional sufficient restriction and possible upper-to-lower path; C claims spectral splitting is established by color alone, and D denies that necessity. Inversion, scene objects and opposite-wall geometry correspond.

questionReviews.observationBoundary: This is a conditional image-formation explanation, not inspection of a real aperture, a figure or a literal spectrum. No new evidence clears d280's HOLD if a literal spectrum is required.

taskFidelity.evidence: C preserves the finite emitter, the head/feet-to-ground comparison and the direction of penumbra-width change in one complete explanation. These are the original causal relationships, not a replacement brightness calculation.

redundancy.evidence: The four alternatives distinguish point versus finite source, reversal of the distance effect, the correct distance effect and denial of any width effect. This source is not split into isolated foot/head clicks.

answerLeakage.evidence: The stem supplies the source's sharp-foot/blurred-head observation, not finite-source penumbra geometry. B and C have parallel wording but opposite width predictions, so the emitting-region phrase alone cannot reveal C.

mathematics.independentSolution: Use d280's finite-source edge geometry w approximately equals D b/a: feet have very small object-to-screen distance b, whereas the head has larger b, normally with a smaller source-to-object distance a. C gives narrower foot and wider head penumbrae. Setting emitter size D to zero removes this source-size penumbra; reversing the trend or denying the width effect is false.

optionChecks.evidence: An ideal geometric point source has zero emitting width, so distance from the ground alone cannot produce a source-size penumbra.
For the usual finite-source geometry, bringing the blocking edge nearer its ground screen shrinks, not widens, the spread of shadow edges. The foot/head trend is reversed.
Finite source points give different projected edges; the short foot-to-ground distance yields a narrow penumbra, and the larger head-to-ground distance yields a wider one.
Changing b/a changes the separation of the finite-source edge projections and hence penumbra width, not only overall shadow size.

bilingual.evidence: Both /3 arrays preserve ideal point source in A, finite emitter in B/C/D, the reversed trend in B and the correct trend in C. Usual streetlamp-shadow scope corresponds.

taskFidelity.evidence: The paired source distances are retained rather than reduced to one endpoint. The nonzero-tilt case C and zero-direct-illuminance case D preserve the original second question with its necessary nondegeneracy boundary. These conditions do not replace the location computation.

redundancy.evidence: A and C repeat the distance pair because the second source subquestion asks whether that same location changes; C additionally requires the common positive incidence factor. D/E test uniqueness when that factor is zero. The repeated pair is disclosed within-question coupling, not an independent extra numerical task or a cross-question dependency.

answerLeakage.evidence: A,C,E repeat 1.6/2.0, but repetition alone neither verifies those distances against 80/125 nor decides the nonzero-versus-zero tilt claims. D/E cannot be settled by counting the repeated pair. The stem does not supply the balance equation or a solved tilt explanation; no separate key exposure is established.

mathematics.independentSolution: Reuse the d280 positive-distance ratio x/(3.6-x)=sqrt(80/125)=4/5 and its established solution 1.6/2.0. At the central patch, opposite source directions and opposite receiving-face normals give the same cosine. A common positive cosine cancels in equality, supporting C. If the screen plane is parallel to the source line, the normal is perpendicular to both rays: cosine zero, both direct values zero at any interior point, supporting D and falsifying uniqueness E.
mathematics.modelScope: Small central ideal receiving element; sources illuminate opposite faces. The given intensities are toward that element and comparisons are direct illuminance, without additional reflected/background/transmitted contributions. This is not a uniform-illuminance claim over every point of a finite screen.

optionChecks.evidence: The distances are the verified d280 solution, sum to 3.6 m and give the required positive ratio 4/5. Its established normal illuminances are both 31.25 lx.
The reversed pair has distance ratio 2.0/1.6=5/4, not the required 4/5. Unequal intensities require the weaker source to be nearer the balance screen, not farther.
Opposite rays and opposite normals have equal positive cosines. Multiplying both normal illuminances by that common nonzero factor leaves the same equality and distance pair.
A plane parallel to the joining line is edge-on to both incident rays. Its ideal projected receiving area is zero, so equality is 0=0 for all interior locations, not a unique balance point.
At zero cosine no positive factor can be cancelled to recover the unique non-grazing equation. Another interior location also has zero on both sides, contradicting uniqueness.

bilingual.evidence: Both /4 arrays bind each distance to the same source intensity. C explicitly requires both direct illuminances nonzero; D specifies the ideal plane element and nonunique interior equality; E asserts the same false uniqueness.

1216/45 and 1200/(13 sqrt(13)) are the two already independently verified d280 totals, including both lamps and each oblique projection.
200/9 keeps only the lamp directly above the point, dropping the positive 24/5 contribution. 600/(13 sqrt(13)) is one midpoint lamp's contribution instead of the sum of two.

findings.observation: The intended conditional prediction that the side observer does not see the beam when visible side scattering is negligible has no true visible option. The surviving true options give only a necessary eye-light condition and a general dependence on scattering/detection.
findings.counterexample: A learner believing that a clean-air beam is normally visible side-on may still correctly choose A,D: that learner can require light in the eye, accept detectability dependence, reject clean means literally zero scattering, and distinguish the front hole from the exit. The source prediction remains untested.
findings.requiredResolution: Preserve an explicit, physically qualified visibility prediction tied to the given side-view setup. Do not equate clean air with exact zero scattering or turn the source into only a question about unspecified conditions. This report does not edit or propose an approved replacement draft.
